title: manni citations vocabulary v1.3.0
description: What do this page's claims rest on? For each claim, the page lines that make it, the source lines it was written from, and a hash of each. A manni common vocabulary: any drift check can implement it, and other schemas may compose on top of it. A pin is a record of the past, not a copy of the present. It says what the lines were when the sentence was written. The check compares that record with the files as they are now. Recompute it on every run and there is nothing to compare against. `source-of-truth` (manni:stewardship:1.0.0) names the file a page answers to; a citation names the lines a sentence answers to. The page root stays open so sibling tools' keys pass untouched. The `citation-` prefix is reserved, so an unrecognized `citation-*` key is rejected and a typo fails loudly. Version 1.1.0 added `last-verified` and `verified-by` to an entry, for a check that proves the pin (proposal 0098). Version 1.2.0 added `repo` to a source, for a file in another checkout (proposal 0100). Version 1.3.0 adds `pointer` to a claim, for a claim that is a metadata value (proposal 0108). An entry is otherwise validated as in 1.2.0.

citations.description: The page's citations, one entry per claim or pin. An empty list is not a declaration; a page with no citations omits the key. Ids are unique within a page, and two entries claiming one id is an error. JSON Schema cannot say that over a list whose members may omit the id. So it is a requirement on implementations, stated here so every tool agrees.

citationEntry.description: One citation: the page text it supports, the source lines it rests on, and how the two are anchored. Both ends share one shape, a line range and a hash.

id.description: A kebab-case name for this citation, unique within the page. A body marker names an entry by it, and findings are reported under it. Optional for an entry anchored by its claim lines or pinned bare. Required when a marker names the entry.

quote.description: The claim is a fenced block that reproduces the source lines. The pinned claim covers the whole block, fences included. An implementer compares the lines inside the fences with the source under the pin's rule. So a quoted snippet that drifts from its source is a finding even while the pin still holds. Under a marker, the block is the next fence after the marker. Default false.

last-verified.description: A day such as 2026-10-21, or a timestamp with a timezone such as 2026-10-21T14:02:11Z. The date by which every check in `verified-by` had passed. It is the oldest `passed` among the entries, set only once every entry has one. One lagging check holds it back, so it never claims more than the checks proved. The verifying tool writes it in the same write as its own entry. A failed check leaves it alone, and its age is the signal.

verified-by.description: The checks that verify this pin, one entry per check. The author lists each entry, and each tool fills in its own entries when its check passes. A tool finds its work by the entries that name it, so no key is tool-specific. This is where a measured fact's attribution lives. `meta-provenance` keeps its own meaning: values a model proposed that no person has reviewed yet.

claim.description: The page text or metadata value the citation supports, pinned by its place and a hash. `lines` places body text and `pointer` places a metadata value. A claim takes one of them, never both. Absent, the entry is a bare pin, or a marker with no drift check on its sentence. With neither, the text pinned is what a body marker naming this entry anchors.

lines.description: Lines of the page body. The body starts on the first line after the closing frontmatter fence, or on line 1 with no frontmatter. So editing the frontmatter never moves a claim. Required unless a marker names the entry or `pointer` is set, and never inside the frontmatter.

pointer.description: A JSON Pointer (RFC 6901) to one value in the page's own metadata, such as `/pains/0`. Write `~` as `~0` and `/` as `~1`. Array indexes count from 0. It never names the whole block, and never anything under `citations`.

integrity.description: `sha256-` and sixty-four lowercase hex digits. Over claimed lines, it follows the rule `source.integrity` states. Over a `pointer`'s value, it is the SHA-256 of the value's canonical JSON under RFC 8785, as UTF-8. Always plain, never keyed: the page is public, so there is nothing to hide. With a marker, the lines hashed are the ones the marker anchors.

source.description: The lines the claim rests on: a file, an optional line range, a pin, and the commit the pin was taken at.

repo.description: The checkout `file` is in, by the name the citing repository's configuration gives it. It is a name, not a path or a URL, so each repository that cites the checkout maps it to a directory of its own. Absent, `file` is in the checkout sources resolve from by default.

lines.description: File lines. Absent, the whole file is pinned. The lines stay readable even when `file` is encrypted.

integrity.description: The pin: an algorithm prefix and sixty-four lowercase hex digits over the cited lines under one rule. Decode as UTF-8 and drop one leading byte-order mark. Turn CRLF into LF, split on LF, and discard the empty element a trailing LF leaves. Take lines L1 to L2 inclusive, or every line for a whole file. Join with LF and no trailing LF, and keep trailing whitespace. A plain `file` is pinned `sha256-` over that text. An encrypted `file` is pinned `hmac-sha256-`: the HMAC-SHA256 of that text under a key derived from the encryption key. So a public page carries no verifier a reader could run against a guessed private line. The prefix follows `file`, and any other pairing is an invalid entry.

commit-sha.description: The git commit hash the source pin was taken at, as lowercase hex. Seven digits is what git abbreviates to; sixty-four covers a SHA-256 repository. A tool writes the full hash, because an abbreviation that is unique today need not be next year. Without it, a check can still say the lines changed. With it, the check can say since when, and whether the pin was ever true.

lines.description: A line range, 1-based and inclusive: an integer for one line, or `"L1-L2"` for several. `L1 <= L2` is a rule on implementations, since a pattern cannot compare two numbers. There is no line 0 to cite.

fileRef.description: The file: a path relative to the repository root, posix-separated, and free of `.` and `..` segments. Segments may hold spaces and dots but not `/`, `\`, `:` or a line break. So a URL, a drive letter, a Windows path and an absolute path all fail here. In place of the path, `~` and at least 82 base64url characters is the path encrypted with the family key. The construction is the family's one ciphertext format. Only a checkout with the key and the files can decrypt the path and read the lines. So a public docs repo can cite a private code repo without publishing its paths. The value carries no encryption mark, because the citation tool encrypts it, and a plain path stays valid.

verification.description: One check that verifies the thing it sits on. The author writes `tool`, and `check` where the tool needs one. The tool writes `version` and `passed` when the check passes, and only then.

tool.description: Each entry names the verifier in tool. The value is the verifier's package name, such as `doc-detective`, or a URL.

check.description: The verifier's own id for the check: a test, spec or rule id. The author writes it, and it is the anchor a tool looks for. An entry without one means the tool verifies the whole thing however it does.

version.description: The verifier's version on the last pass. The tool writes it in the same write as `passed`.

passed.description: A day such as 2026-10-21, or a timestamp with a timezone such as 2026-10-21T14:02:11Z. When this check last passed. The tool writes it on a pass and leaves it alone on a failure, so its age is the signal.

verifiedDate.description: A day, `YYYY-MM-DD`, or an RFC 3339 timestamp with seconds and a required timezone, such as `2026-10-21T14:02:11Z`. A month alone fails, and so does a local time with no offset. Field-ranged, not calendar-exact.
